questions.question: A cart moves along a straight horizontal track. Its velocity-time graph is a straight line decreasing from v = +10 m/s at t = 0 to v = -10 m/s at t = 4 s. What is the cart's acceleration?
questions.explanation: Acceleration is defined as the rate of change of velocity with respect to time, which corresponds directly to the slope of a velocity-time graph: a = Δv / Δt. Here, the velocity decreases uniformly from v_initial = +10 m/s at t = 0 to v_final = -10 m/s at t = 4 s. Substituting into the slope formula: a = (-10 - 10) / (4 - 0) = -20 / 4 = -5.0 m/s^2. The negative sign denotes constant deceleration in the positive direction followed by acceleration in the negative direction.
questions.citation: College Board AP® Physics 1 CED — Topic 1.2 Representations of Motion

questions.question: A projectile is launched with initial velocity v0 at an angle θ above the horizontal on level ground. Neglecting air resistance, what happens to the projectile's horizontal velocity component during its flight?
options: It decreases to zero at the peak of the trajectory and then increases
It constantly accelerates at 9.8 m/s^2 downward
It increases continuously until the projectile impacts the ground
It remains constant at v0 * cos(θ) because there is zero net horizontal force
questions.explanation: Because air resistance is neglected, gravity acts purely in the vertical direction (ay = -g). There is zero net force horizontally (ax = 0), so horizontal velocity vx = v0 * cos(θ) remains strictly constant throughout flight.
questions.citation: College Board AP® Physics 1 CED — Topic 1.3 Projectile Motion

questions.question: Two blocks with masses m1 = 2 kg and m2 = 3 kg are connected by a light string on a frictionless horizontal tabletop. A horizontal pulling force F = 15 N is applied to m2. What is the tension in the connecting string?
questions.explanation: Total system acceleration a = F_net / (m1 + m2) = 15 / (2 + 3) = 15 / 5 = 3.0 m/s^2. The only horizontal force accelerating m1 is the string tension T: T = m1 * a = 2 kg * 3.0 m/s^2 = 6.0 N.
questions.citation: College Board AP® Physics 1 CED — Topic 2.4 Newton's Second Law

questions.question: The Earth exerts an attractive gravitational force of magnitude F_E on the Moon. What gravitational force does the Moon exert on the Earth?
options: A much smaller force because the Moon's mass is smaller than Earth's
Zero force because the Earth's gravitational field dominates
An equal force of magnitude F_E directed toward the Moon
A force that varies inversely with the Moon's orbital period
questions.explanation: According to Newton's Third Law of Motion, every action force produces an equal and opposite reaction force between the two interacting bodies. Thus, the Moon exerts an identical force F_E on the Earth directed toward the Moon.
questions.citation: College Board AP® Physics 1 CED — Topic 2.7 Newton's Third Law

questions.question: A crate of mass M rests on a rough inclined ramp. As the ramp's inclination angle θ is gradually increased, the crate begins to slip when θ reaches 30°. What is the coefficient of static friction μ_s between crate and ramp?
questions.explanation: At the threshold of impending slipping: F_gravity_parallel = F_friction_max → M*g*sin(θ) = μ_s * (M*g*cos(θ)). Dividing both sides by M*g*cos(θ) gives μ_s = sin(θ) / cos(θ) = tan(θ). At θ = 30°, μ_s = tan(30°) ≈ 0.577.
questions.citation: College Board AP® Physics 1 CED — Topic 2.6 Friction

questions.subtopic: Centripetal Acceleration & Flat Curves (Unit 3: Circular Motion)
questions.question: A car of mass m rounds an unbanked flat circular curve of radius R at constant speed v. What physical force provides the necessary centripetal acceleration toward the center of the curve?
options: The kinetic friction force between tires and asphalt
The normal force acting vertically upward from the road
The centrifugal force pushing outward on the vehicle
The static friction force exerted by the roadway on the car's tires
questions.explanation: On an unbanked curve, the normal force and gravity act vertically and balance out. The only horizontal force directed toward the center of the circular path is the static friction force between the tire treads and the road surface.
questions.citation: College Board AP® Physics 1 CED — Topic 3.2 Centripetal Acceleration and Force

questions.question: Two spherical satellites are separated by center-to-center distance r and experience gravitational attraction F. If the separation distance between the satellites is doubled to 2r, what is the new gravitational force?
questions.explanation: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation: F = G * (m1 * m2) / r^2. If r is replaced by 2r: F_new = G * (m1 * m2) / (2r)^2 = F / 4. Gravitational force follows an inverse-square law.
questions.citation: College Board AP® Physics 1 CED — Topic 3.3 Gravitational Fields

questions.question: A net horizontal force F acts on a 4.0 kg object initially at rest on a frictionless surface. If the force does 72 Joules of work on the object, what is the object's final velocity?
questions.citation: College Board AP® Physics 1 CED — Topic 4.2 Work and Mechanical Energy

questions.question: A roller coaster car of mass m rolls without friction into a vertical circular loop of radius R. What is the minimum speed the car must have at the top of the loop so it does not lose contact with the track?
questions.explanation: At the very top of the loop, the minimum speed occurs when the normal force drops to zero (N = 0). Gravity alone supplies the centripetal force: m*g = m*v^2 / R → g = v^2 / R → v = √(g * R).
questions.citation: College Board AP® Physics 1 CED — Topic 4.3 Conservation of Energy

questions.question: A spring with force constant k = 200 N/m is compressed by 0.10 m. What is the elastic potential energy stored in the compressed spring?
questions.explanation: The elastic potential energy stored in an ideal Hookean spring compressed or stretched by a distance x from its uncompressed equilibrium length is given by Us = (1/2) * k * x^2. Given spring constant k = 200 N/m and compression distance x = 0.10 m: Us = (1/2) * (200 N/m) * (0.10 m)^2 = 100 * 0.01 = 1.0 Joule. This represents the total mechanical work performed against the spring restoring force.
questions.citation: College Board AP® Physics 1 CED — Topic 4.1 Systems and Energy

questions.question: An electric crane lifts a 500 kg steel girder vertically at a constant speed of 2.0 m/s. Assuming g = 10 m/s^2, what is the power output delivered by the crane motor?
questions.explanation: Lifting at constant velocity requires upward force equal to weight: F = m*g = 500 kg * 10 m/s^2 = 5,000 N. Power P = F * v = 5,000 N * 2.0 m/s = 10,000 Watts (10 kW).
questions.citation: College Board AP® Physics 1 CED — Topic 4.4 Power

questions.question: A 2.0 kg cart traveling to the right at 6.0 m/s collides with and sticks to a stationary 4.0 kg cart on a frictionless track. What is the velocity of the combined carts after the collision?
questions.explanation: Conservation of linear momentum: m1*v1 + m2*v2 = (m1 + m2)*v_final. (2.0)(6.0) + (4.0)(0) = (2.0 + 4.0)*v_final → 12.0 = 6.0 * v_final → v_final = 2.0 m/s to the right.
questions.citation: College Board AP® Physics 1 CED — Topic 5.2 Momentum and Impulse

questions.question: A baseball of mass 0.15 kg traveling horizontally at 40 m/s is struck by a bat and rebounds horizontally in the opposite direction at 50 m/s. What is the magnitude of the impulse delivered to the ball?
questions.explanation: Impulse J = Δp = m * (v_final - v_initial). Setting initial direction as positive (+40 m/s), final velocity is -50 m/s: J = 0.15 * (-50 - 40) = 0.15 * (-90) = -13.5 N·s. The magnitude of the impulse is 13.5 N·s.
questions.citation: College Board AP® Physics 1 CED — Topic 5.1 Momentum and Impulse

questions.question: Two particles of masses m1 = 1.0 kg and m2 = 3.0 kg are located along the x-axis at x1 = 0 m and x2 = 8.0 m. Where is the center of mass of the system located?
questions.explanation: The center of mass for a one-dimensional system of discrete particles is calculated using the weighted average formula: x_cm = (m1*x1 + m2*x2) / (m1 + m2). Substituting the given values m1 = 1.0 kg at x1 = 0 m and m2 = 3.0 kg at x2 = 8.0 m: x_cm = ((1.0 * 0) + (3.0 * 8.0)) / (1.0 + 3.0) = 24.0 / 4.0 = 6.0 m. The center of mass is located at x = 6.0 m, which is 3 times closer to the heavier 3.0 kg particle than to the 1.0 kg particle.
questions.citation: College Board AP® Physics 1 CED — Topic 5.3 Conservation of Linear Momentum

questions.subtopic: Rotational Static Equilibrium (Unit 7: Torque and Rotational Motion)
questions.question: A uniform horizontal beam of length 4.0 m and weight 200 N is pivoted at its center. A 300 N weight is placed 1.0 m to the left of the pivot. Where must a 150 N weight be placed to balance the beam in static equilibrium?
options: 2.0 m to the right of the pivot
1.5 m to the right of the pivot
1.0 m to the right of the pivot
2.5 m to the right of the pivot
questions.explanation: For rotational equilibrium, net torque Στ = 0 about the pivot. Counter-clockwise torque from 300 N: τ_ccw = 300 N * 1.0 m = 300 N·m. Clockwise torque: τ_cw = 150 N * d. Setting equal: 150 * d = 300 → d = 2.0 m to the right of the pivot.
questions.citation: College Board AP® Physics 1 CED — Topic 7.1 Rotational Kinematics and Torque

questions.subtopic: Rotational Inertia of Rolling Objects (Unit 7: Rotational Motion)
questions.question: A solid cylinder (I = (1/2)MR^2) and a thin-walled hollow hoop (I = MR^2) of identical mass M and radius R are released simultaneously from rest at the top of an inclined ramp and roll down without slipping. Which reaches the bottom first?
options: The hollow hoop reaches the bottom first because it has greater rotational kinetic energy
Both reach the bottom at the exact same instant because their masses and radii are identical
The solid cylinder reaches the bottom first because it has a smaller rotational inertia fraction
It depends on the value of static friction between the objects and the ramp
questions.explanation: Acceleration of a rolling object down an incline is a = (g*sin(θ)) / (1 + I/(MR^2)). For solid cylinder, I/(MR^2) = 0.5 (a = g*sin(θ)/1.5). For hollow hoop, I/(MR^2) = 1.0 (a = g*sin(θ)/2.0). The solid cylinder accelerates faster and reaches the bottom first.
questions.citation: College Board AP® Physics 1 CED — Topic 7.3 Rotational Dynamics and Energy

questions.subtopic: Conservation of Angular Momentum (Unit 7: Rotational Motion)
questions.question: A figure skater spinning on frictionless ice pulls her outstretched arms inward toward her torso. What happens to her rotational inertia (I), angular velocity (ω), and rotational kinetic energy (K_rot)?
options: I decreases, ω increases, and K_rot remains constant
I increases, ω decreases, and K_rot decreases
I remains constant, while ω and K_rot both double
I decreases, ω increases, and K_rot increases due to internal work done by her muscles
questions.explanation: Pulling arms inward brings mass closer to rotation axis, reducing rotational inertia I. Because net external torque is zero, angular momentum L = I*ω is conserved, so ω must increase. Rotational kinetic energy K_rot = L^2 / (2I); as I decreases, K_rot increases because the skater does internal mechanical work pulling against centrifugal effects.
questions.citation: College Board AP® Physics 1 CED — Topic 7.4 Conservation of Angular Momentum

questions.subtopic: Mass-Spring Simple Harmonic Motion (Unit 6: Simple Harmonic Motion)
questions.question: An ideal mass-spring system on a frictionless horizontal surface oscillates with period T. If the attached mass m is quadrupled to 4m while keeping spring constant k unchanged, what is the new oscillation period?
questions.explanation: The period of oscillation for an ideal mass-spring system in simple harmonic motion is given by T = 2*pi * √(m / k). If the oscillating mass is quadrupled to 4m while keeping the spring constant k unchanged, the new period becomes: T_new = 2*pi * √(4m / k) = √(4) * [2*pi * √(m / k)] = 2T. Because period scales proportionally with the square root of the inertial mass, quadrupling the mass exactly doubles the period.
questions.citation: College Board AP® Physics 1 CED — Topic 6.1 Period of Simple Harmonic Oscillators

questions.subtopic: Simple Pendulum Period (Unit 6: Simple Harmonic Motion)
questions.question: A simple pendulum of length L and bob mass m oscillates with small amplitude and period T. If the bob is replaced with one of mass 3m while keeping length L constant, what is the new period of oscillation?
questions.explanation: The small-angle period of a simple pendulum is T = 2π * √(L / g). Notice that mass m does not appear anywhere in the period equation; the period depends exclusively on pendulum length and local gravitational acceleration.
questions.citation: College Board AP® Physics 1 CED — Topic 6.2 Simple Pendulum Dynamics

questions.subtopic: Standing Waves on a String (Unit 6: Harmonic Waves)
questions.question: A guitar string of length L is fixed at both ends and vibrates in its fundamental mode (first harmonic). What is the wavelength λ of the standing wave on the string?
questions.explanation: In the fundamental mode of a string fixed at both ends, nodes occur at the ends and an antinode at the center, representing half a wavelength: L = λ / 2 → λ = 2L.
questions.citation: College Board AP® Physics 1 CED — Topic 6.3 Wave Properties & Standing Waves
